To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the gradient of an empirical risk function can be approximated by an element of a low dimensional subspace of the ambient space and that the dimension of this subspace can be bounded in terms of the smoothness of the function and the size of the data set.

1) the privacy of the data is preserved in a distributed setting; 2) a distributed algorithm can be used for the analysis of the data without the knowledge of the underlying distribution of the data; 3) the distributed algorithm can be applied to the analysis of data in the presence of a privacy constraint.

(i) we provide an algorithm that, given a subspace $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a target $\epsilon$, outputs a vector $v$ with $\|v\|\le 1$ and $\|v-U\|_{\infty} \le \epsilon$ with constant probability and (ii) we provide a generalization of the algorithm to a more general class of subspaces and show how this algorithm can be used for private optimization.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following problem: given access to a database of size n over a universe of size d, can we identify a subspace of dimension k, where k << d, that is a good approximation to the true subspace of interest?
the question: Can we learn a low-dimensional structure of a private data set, and if so, how?
understanding how to leverage the low dimensional structure of data in private data analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data privacy literature does not have a clear consensus on the privacy definition that is the most appropriate to use in a specific application.
there is no known algorithm for privately learning subspaces, and it is not clear that such an algorithm can exist.
there is not enough data to support a conclusive statement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the subspace structure is not only useful for improving the utility of the learning algorithms, but also can be used for improving the privacy of the learning algorithms.
we can learn low-dimensional subspaces of high-dimensional spaces, while preserving differential privacy.
we show that the low-dimensional subspace can be identified with a small amount of data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the curse of dimensionality can be overcome by identifying the underlying structure of the data.
we can learn the subspace structure privately, with only a small loss in accuracy.
the privacy-accuracy trade-off is not as bad as it seems, if we have a good prior on the data distribution.
